synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-c.formal:
Let the descent deposit, on the comoving slice of the descent, a scalar perturbation $\zeta$ whose two-point function is homogeneous and isotropic, $C(r) = \langle\zeta(\vec x)\zeta(\vec x + \vec r)\rangle$, with one-point variance $\sigma^{2} = C(0)$, power spectrum $P(k) = \int C(r)e^{-I_4\vec k\cdot\vec r}\,d^{3}r$ (the Fourier transform of a scalar function, valued in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, conventions U1) and dimensionless spectrum $\Delta^{2}(k) = k^{3}P(k)/2\pi^{2}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Finite range.)} If $C(r) = 0$ for $r > R$ (comoving), then for every $k$, $\Delta^{2}(k) \le \tfrac{2}{3\pi}\,\sigma^{2}(kR)^{3}$. If instead $|C(r)| \le \sigma^{2}e^{-r/\xi}$, then $\Delta^{2}(k) \le \tfrac{4}{\pi}\,\sigma^{2}(k\xi)^{3}$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(No exit after the descent.)} Let the descended phase, from the descent to today, be a flat FLRW universe with $\dot a^{2}/H_{0}^{2} = \Omega_{r}a^{-2} + \Omega_{m}a^{-1} + \Omega_{\Lambda}a^{2}$ ($a_{0} = 1$, $\Omega_{m} = 0.315$, $\Omega_{r} = 9.2 \times 10^{-5}$, $\Omega_{\Lambda} = 1 - \Omega_{m} - \Omega_{r}$, the record values of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}). Then $\dot a$ decreases on $(0, \tfrac12]$ and $\dot a \le H_{0}$ on $[\tfrac12, 1]$, so a mode with $k > a_{0}H_{0}$ that is outside the Hubble length at the descent enters once and never leaves it again before today. The pivot $k_{*} = 0.05\ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ has $k_{*}/a_{0}H_{0} \in (222, 223)$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The range needed.)} With the descent at reheating temperature $T_{d}$, at least $1$ MeV by the nucleosynthesis floor (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-bbn-reheating-temperature-floor}), and radiation domination from it (entropy conserved), $\rho(T_{d}) := a_{d}H_{d}/a_{0}H_{0}$ exceeds $4.9 \times 10^{7}$ at $T_{d} = 1$ MeV and $7.2 \times 10^{22}$ at $T_{d} = 10^{12}$ GeV, so the pivot lies outside the descent's Hubble length by more than $2.2 \times 10^{5}$ and $3.2 \times 10^{20}$ respectively. If the pivot's primordial amplitude, $\Delta^{2}(k_{*}) = A_{s} \ge 2.0 \times 10^{-9}$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}: $(2.100 \pm 0.030) \times 10^{-9}$), is the deposit's, carried unchanged outside the Hubble length as an adiabatic $\zeta$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-superhorizon-zeta-conservation}), and $\sigma^{2} \le 1$, then (i) requires $R > 460/(a_{d}H_{d})$ at $T_{d} = 1$ MeV and $R > 6.8 \times 10^{17}/(a_{d}H_{d})$ at $T_{d} = 10^{12}$ GeV (and a clustering length $\xi > 250/(a_{d}H_{d})$ at $1$ MeV); the required range grows linearly with $T_{d}$ in units of the descent's Hubble length. In comoving units it is one length for every $T_{d}$: (i) gives $k_{*}R > (3\pi A_{s}/2)^{1/3}$, so $a_{0}H_{0}R > (3\pi A_{s}/2)^{1/3}\,a_{0}H_{0}/k_{*}$, about $9.5 \times 10^{-6}$ of the present Hubble radius (about $42$ kpc comoving; in $(9.4, 9.8) \times 10^{-6}$ over the recorded band of $A_{s}$, Proposition \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-descent-as-vacuum}(ii)), and the $T_{d}$ dependence above is that of the unit $1/(a_{d}H_{d})$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Scope of the frozen-phase results.)} If the frozen phase is the de Sitter stage of the observed $\Lambda$, $H_{\Lambda} = \sqrt{\Lambda/3} = H_{0}\sqrt{\Omega_{\Lambda}}$, the temperature of whose horizon is Theorem \claimref{synthesis.de-sitter-temperature-frozen-point-norm}'s $T_{\Lambda}$, then the pivot mode leaves that phase's Hubble length only at $a > 268\,a_{0}$, in the future: the late-time boundary on which Proposition \claimref{synthesis.frozen-phase-spectrum-not-red} reads the index is not where the measured spectrum was set.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, in the series' history as the dating reads it (descent at the origin, no inflationary stage), a primordial spectrum of the measured amplitude at the pivot from the descent's deposit, passive and with $\sigma^{2} \le 1$, needs correlations over hundreds to about $10^{18}$ Hubble lengths of the descent, set before or outside the descended metric; a deposit whose $\zeta$ has finite range at the Hubble or thermal length gives $\Delta^{2} \propto (kR)^{3}$ there, index $n_{s} - 1 = 3$ in the limit, and an amplitude far below $A_{s}$. Whether a matter deposit of finite range has a $\zeta$ of finite range depends on the expansion datum of the descent slice, which the series leaves free (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.descent-slice-constraints-and-the-three-readings-of-a-white-deposit}): under its reading (FR), a flat slice with the deposit at rest on it, it does; under (FM), a flat slice with the deposit's own momentum noise, the index is $+1$; under (UE), a slice of uniform expansion, the $\zeta$ is the potential of the matter excess, of infinite range, with index $-1$.

\emph{Note (pointer).} Two later results bear on a deposit that is not passive but classically modulated by a field: such a modulation is adiabatic only along a local time shift of the one descent, so the carrier is a field of delays, itself still subject to the bound of (i) (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.adiabatic-deposit-modulation-is-a-time-shift}); and a local conversion of a Gaussian modulating field into the curvature perturbation cannot lower the field's index, so under hypothesis (F) a Gaussian modulator read through the frozen point's invariant state gives index $2$ up to corrections of order $(k|x_{d}|)^{-2}$ (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.local-conversion-cannot-redden-a-gaussian-spectator}). The classical-modulation escape is therefore closed for Gaussian modulators; a red or non-Gaussian modulator is not covered.
synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-c.technical:
The bound is the causality (white-noise) argument in its simplest form: the power spectrum of a field with correlations of finite range is bounded by the integral of the absolute correlation, at most the variance times the range volume, so the dimensionless spectrum falls as the cube of $kR$ on scales larger than the range, whatever the tilt inside it. The horizon arithmetic is standard: in a descended phase that decelerates until the dark-energy era, comoving Hubble lengths only grow, so a mode at the pivot was outside the descent's Hubble length by the factor $\rho(T_{d})/222$ and, once inside, never leaves. Exact rational bounds with record inputs give the factors in (iii).

So a descent can seed the measured spectrum only through a deposit whose correlations reach hundreds of Hubble lengths of the descent at the lowest reheating temperature nucleosynthesis allows (at least $1.8$ MeV, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-bbn-reheating-temperature-floor}, used here in the weaker form $1$ MeV) and about $10^{18}$ at the heavy-neutrino scales the store uses for $T_{\mathrm{desc}}$. These are one comoving length, about $9.5 \times 10^{-6}$ of the present Hubble radius, at every reheating temperature: what grows with the temperature is the descent's Hubble length used as the unit. Such correlations are not produced by anything inside the descended metric; they are initial data of the pre-metric sector. The pure-pair deposit of the quadratic-flows result, and any deposit that is locally the I-state and clusters at the thermal length, fall under (i) where their $\zeta$ has finite range, which for a matter deposit of finite range is the flat-slice reading (FR) of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.descent-slice-constraints-and-the-three-readings-of-a-white-deposit} and does not hold on a slice of uniform expansion. The stored frozen-phase no-gos, read at $H = H_{\Lambda}$, concern modes that leave the horizon only in the far future. Active causal sources after the descent are not covered; their incoherent acoustic peaks are excluded by the measured spectrum as a dominant source (cited from memory, not used).
synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-c.lay: In this theory the universe begins with a descent event rather than with inflation. The temperature ripples in the cosmic background were, at the moment of the descent, spread over distances far larger than anything that could have been in causal contact then. If a deposit's ripples are correlated only up to a finite distance, it gives ripples on much larger scales that are weaker by the cube of the ratio (whether matter laid down with correlations of finite reach makes ripples of finite reach depends on how each region starts expanding, which the theory leaves open), so to produce the observed ripples the descent's initial state must already be correlated over hundreds to a billion billion of its own horizon lengths. Either the pre-spacetime phase supplies such long-range order, or a source acting after the descent does (which the observed acoustic peaks disfavour), or the theory cannot produce the observed spectrum.

proofs.main:
(i) $|P(k)| \le \int|C(r)|\,d^{3}r$. A covariance satisfies $|C(r)| \le C(0)$ (the Gram matrix of $\zeta(\vec x)$ and $\zeta(\vec x + \vec r)$ is positive semidefinite). With support in $r \le R$, $\int|C|\,d^{3}r \le \sigma^{2}\cdot\tfrac{4\pi}{3}R^{3}$, so $\Delta^{2}(k) \le k^{3}\sigma^{2}\tfrac{4\pi}{3}R^{3}/(2\pi^{2}) = \tfrac{2}{3\pi}\sigma^{2}(kR)^{3}$. With $|C| \le \sigma^{2}e^{-r/\xi}$, $\int|C|\,d^{3}r \le 4\pi\sigma^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{2}e^{-r/\xi}dr = 8\pi\sigma^{2}\xi^{3}$ (antiderivative $-\xi(r^{2} + 2r\xi + 2\xi^{2})e^{-r/\xi}$), so $\Delta^{2}(k) \le \tfrac{4}{\pi}\sigma^{2}(k\xi)^{3}$. For compact support $P$ is moreover an even entire function of $k$, $P(k) = \sum_{j}(-1)^{j}k^{2j}m_{2j}/(2j+1)!$ with $m_{2j} = 4\pi\int r^{2j+2}C\,dr$, so as $kR \to 0$ the local index $d\ln\Delta^{2}/d\ln k$ tends to $3 + 2j_{0}$, $j_{0}$ the first nonvanishing moment, unless $C \equiv 0$: $n_{s} - 1 \to 3$ or more. This is the white-noise form of the causality argument, standard in cosmology (from memory; not imported, since the step above is self-contained).

(ii) $f(a) = \dot a^{2}/H_{0}^{2}$ has $a^{3}f'(a) = g(a) = -2\Omega_{r} - \Omega_{m}a + 2\Omega_{\Lambda}a^{4}$, convex in $a$, with $g(0) = -2\Omega_{r} < 0$ and $g(\tfrac12) < 0$, hence $g < 0$ and $f$ decreasing on $(0, \tfrac12]$; $f'' > 0$ on $(0, \infty)$, so on $[\tfrac12, 1]$, $f \le \max(f(\tfrac12), f(1)) = f(1) = 1$. A mode $k > a_{0}H_{0}$ outside at the descent ($k < a_{d}H_{d} = \dot a_{d}$) enters at the unique $a_{e} \le \tfrac12$ with $\dot a(a_{e}) = k$ (since $\dot a(\tfrac12) < H_{0} < k$), stays inside while $\dot a$ decreases, and has $k > H_{0} \ge \dot a$ on $[\tfrac12, 1]$. The present-day inputs are the record's (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}: $\Omega_{m} = 0.315$, and $\Omega_{r} = 9.2 \times 10^{-5}$ from $T_{0}$ with three relativistic neutrino species); any decelerating content before the Lambda era (more relativistic species, a matter era of any duration) only strengthens the monotonicity. $k_{*}/a_{0}H_{0} = 0.05 \times 299792.458/67.4 = 149896229/674000 \in (222, 223)$.

(iii) For radiation domination from $T_{d}$ with entropy conservation, $a_{d}/a_{0} = (T_{0}/T_{d})(g_{s}(T_{0})/g_{s}(T_{d}))^{1/3}$ and $H_{d} = \pi\sqrt{g_{*}/90}\,T_{d}^{2}/M_{P}$ (reduced Planck mass, $g_{s} = g_{*}$ at $T_{d}$). The check bounds $\rho^{6}$ below with $\pi > 3$ and exact rational record inputs ($T_{0} = 2.7255$ K and $H_{0} = 67.4$ km/s/Mpc from Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}, the reduced Planck mass $M_{P} = 2.435 \times 10^{18}$ GeV, $g_{s}(T_{0}) = 43/11$, $g_{*} = 10.75$ at $1$ MeV and $106.75$ at $10^{12}$ GeV): $4.96 \times 10^{7} < \rho(1\ \mathrm{MeV}) < 5.21 \times 10^{7}$, $7.27 \times 10^{22} < \rho(10^{12}\ \mathrm{GeV}) < 7.63 \times 10^{22}$ (with $\pi < 22/7$ for the upper brackets, about $12$ and $47$ e-folds above the pivot after dividing by $222$). Put $R = K/(a_{d}H_{d})$, so $k_{*}R = K k_{*}/(a_{0}H_{0}\rho)$. By (i), $A_{s} \le \Delta^{2}(k_{*}) \le \tfrac{2}{3\pi}\sigma^{2}(k_{*}R)^{3}$ gives $K^{3} \ge \tfrac{3\pi}{2}A_{s}\rho^{3}(a_{0}H_{0}/k_{*})^{3}/\sigma^{2}$; with $\sigma^{2} \le 1$, $A_{s} \ge 2.0 \times 10^{-9}$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}: $(2.100 \pm 0.030) \times 10^{-9}$) and $\pi > 3$ the check gives $K > 460$ and $K > 6.8 \times 10^{17}$, and the clustering version $K' > 250$ at $1$ MeV. $\rho$ is proportional to $T_{d}$ at fixed $g_{*}$ (up to $g_{*}^{1/2}g_{s}^{-1/3}$), and so is $K$. A smaller variance makes the requirement stronger, $K \propto \sigma^{-2/3}$. The premise that the pivot's amplitude is the deposit's is the passive reading: under the dynamics (L$_{E}$) permits, the boundary modes' occupations are conserved after the descent (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.quadratic-flows-cannot-thermalise-descent}), so the deposit is not reprocessed by relaxation; in the descended phase an adiabatic $\zeta$ is conserved outside the Hubble length (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-superhorizon-zeta-conservation}), and by (ii) the pivot is outside it from the descent until it enters. The lowest reheating temperature allowed by nucleosynthesis is $1.8$ MeV for radiative and $4$ to $5$ MeV for hadronic decays (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-bbn-reheating-temperature-floor}); $1$ MeV is used as a weaker bound.

(iv) By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.de-sitter-temperature-frozen-point-norm} the frozen point's horizon has $T_{\Lambda} = \sqrt{\Lambda/3}/2\pi$, the Hubble rate of the frozen phase being $H = \sqrt{\Lambda/3}$; for the observed $\Lambda$, $H_{\Lambda} = H_{0}\sqrt{\Omega_{\Lambda}}$. In that phase a mode leaves the Hubble length when $k = aH_{\Lambda}$; for the pivot this is $a = (k_{*}/a_{0}H_{0})/\sqrt{\Omega_{\Lambda}} \in (268, 269)$. The flat-slicing late-time boundary $x_{0} \to 0$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.frozen-phase-spectrum-not-red} is therefore reached by the pivot mode only in the far future. Whether the frozen phase at the descent is this stage depends on the single frozen point and the dating, which are premises and an observation-level reading respectively; (iv) is stated under that hypothesis only.

Not covered: active sources after the descent (scaling seeds), which can produce flat spectra causally but give incoherent acoustic peaks (from memory); a deposit with $\sigma^{2} > 1$, which is not a perturbation of FLRW.

The check verifies the constants $(4\pi/3)/(2\pi^{2}) = 2/(3\pi)$ and $8\pi/(2\pi^{2}) = 4/\pi$, the antiderivative identity at three values of $\xi$, the $2 \times 2$ Gram condition, the bounds on $\rho^{6}$, $k_{*}/a_{0}H_{0}$ and $K^{6}$ in exact rationals, and the convexity and monotonicity of $f$ for (ii) and the exit scale of (iv).

synthesis.frozen-phase-spectrum-not-red.technical:
In the conformal model the frozen point can be placed at $He_{0}$, a timelike unit direction scaled by $H$; it has the same norm $\Lambda/3$ as the chart frozen point $\nInf + (\Lambda/6)\nO$ and is carried to it by two reflections. Its scale function is $Hx_{0}$, so the metric $\eta/(Hx_{0})^{2}$ is de Sitter space in flat slicing, the late-time boundary being $x_{0} \to 0$. The stabiliser contains the slicing's rotations, spatial translations and the dilatation $X(x) \mapsto \lambda X(x/\lambda)$ generated by $\nO \wedge \nInf$, which leaves the metric invariant. All of this is checked exactly with rotors at rapidity $\ln 4$.

If the late-time perturbation the descent leaves is invariant under those symmetries and scales as a density of weight $w$ (up to a constant at $w = 0$), a two-line scaling argument gives $P(\lambda k) = \lambda^{-3-2w}P(k)$, so $\Delta^{2}(k) \propto k^{-2w}$ and $n_{s} - 1 = -2w$. If moreover the perturbation is the boundary value of a field of the series the store uses, or a local polynomial in such fields, then by the dictionary $m^{2} = -w(w+3)H^{2}$, whose roots are the late-time falloff exponents, its leading weight has real part in $[-3/2, 0]$ and $n_{s} \ge 1$ (on the principal series $n_{s} - 1 = 3$ is the index of an oscillating envelope); the exceptional series gives $n_{s} - 1 \le -2$. The measured $n_{s} = 0.9649$ needs $w \approx 0.018$, a slightly tachyonic $m^{2} \approx -0.053H^{2}$ outside every series, and the scale-invariant floor is about $8.4$ standard deviations away.

Under the Henneaux-Teitelboim promotion the frozen point's norm becomes a field whose constancy is an equation of motion, so it has no fluctuation at nonzero wavenumber. The red tilt must therefore come from the descent's state breaking the slicing dilatation (about $0.018$ per e-fold of scale), from a weight-shifting map to the curvature perturbation such as a fractional inverse gradient, or from a source outside the series' fields.
synthesis.frozen-phase-spectrum-not-red.lay: The measured pattern of the earliest ripples in the universe is almost, but not quite, the same at every size: slightly stronger on large scales. In this framework the universe after the descent sits at a frozen point whose symmetry includes stretching all distances by a common factor, and that symmetry forces any ripple pattern it leaves to follow a simple power law whose slope is fixed by a weight, the same number the series already uses to describe mass. For every kind of field the series uses, that slope is either exactly flat or tilted the wrong way; the observed tilt would need a field with negative mass squared. The frozen point itself cannot ripple from place to place either. synthesis.frozen-point-datum-is-h.technical: With the foundation's scalars in $\Q$ until the completion, the frozen point $I_{\Lambda} = \nInf + \tfrac{\Lambda}{6}\nO$ has square $d = \Lambda/3$, and everything in which $\Lambda$ enters rationally (the norm, the static boost $B_{\Lambda} = e_{0}W$ with $B_{\Lambda}^{2} = d$, the scale $\sigma = 1 - \Lambda Q(x)/12$, the complement $I_{\Lambda}^{\perp} = \langle 1,-1,-1,-1,-d\rangle$) is defined over any field $K$ of characteristic $0$. What needs a square root is a single condition: the boost's null eigen-directions, the unit boost $B_{\Lambda}/H$, the unit vector $W/H$, the horizon radius $R_{h} = 1/H$ and surface gravity $H$, the horizon point $(2/H)e_{1}$ of the observer's slice, the isometry of $I_{\Lambda}^{\perp}$ with the standard $(1,4)$ space, the doubled type $\Cl(1,4)$ and the mirror's $\Cl(4,1)$ each exist over $K$ exactly when $\Lambda/3$ is a square in $K$. Taking $H$ as the datum, $\Lambda = 3H^{2}$, makes them all hold over $K$ as written; over $\R$ nothing changes. Over $\Q$, $\Lambda = 7/3$ loses all of them, the bifurcation sphere having no rational point at all, and $\Lambda = 6$ loses them too, with centres the quadratic fields of discriminants $8$ and $-8$. Five constructions need a condition of their own: a point of the bifurcation sphere ($\Lambda/3$ a sum of three squares), a similarity carrying the frozen point's stabiliser to $SO(1,4)$ ($\Lambda/3$ a sum of two squares, which fails for $\Lambda = 9$), the complexified reading of the mirror ($-1$ not a square, automatic over an ordered field), the sheaf rescaling by $\sqrt{|\Lambda|}$ ($\sqrt{3}$ besides $H$) and the operator join's matched scale ($\sqrt{2}$ besides $H$). On the anti-de Sitter side the datum is $H'$ with $\Lambda = -3H'^{2}$. Statements that need the completion anyway, such as the Euclidean period $2\pi/\kappa_{\Lambda}$, are unaffected.
synthesis.frozen-point-datum-is-h.lay: Before the series passes to the real numbers, its numbers are fractions. The frozen point, the vector that carries the cosmological constant, has squared length one third of that constant, and several constructions built on it (the light-like directions of the horizon's boost, the horizon's radius, the type of algebra the frozen point leaves behind) need the square root of that number. With the cosmological constant itself as the given number they work only for special values; with the expansion rate H as the given number, the constant being three times its square, they all work. A few constructions need a little more, such as the square root of 2 or of 3, and this result says exactly which, and what each needs.

synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-de.formal:
Work in the conformal model of Lemma \claimref{mass.de-sitter-scale-frozen-point} ($\ip{\nO}{\nInf} = 1$, $X(x) = \nO + x - \tfrac12 Q(x)\,\nInf$, $Q$ of signature $(+,-,-,-)$) with the flat-slicing frozen point $I_{\mathrm{fs}} = He_{0}$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.frozen-phase-spectrum-not-red}, $\Lambda = 3H^{2}$, scale function $\ip{X(x)}{I_{\mathrm{fs}}} = Hx_{0}$, so that the frozen point's gravitational field is de Sitter in its flat slicing with conformal time $x_{0} < 0$ and $x_{0} \to 0^{-}$ its future infinity. Let the descended universe be the flat FLRW field of the stored finite-range result on the same flat background, $\hb^{-1}(a) = a(\eta)\,a$ in conformal coordinates $(\eta, \vec x)$, with $\dot a^{2}/H_{0}^{2} = \Omega_{r}a^{-2} + \Omega_{m}a^{-1} + \Omega_{\Lambda}a^{2}$ and the record values of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}. Hypothesis (F): its late-time de Sitter stage is the frozen point's field, $a(\eta) \to 1/(H|x_{0}|)$ with $x_{0} = \eta - \eta_{\infty}$, $\eta_{\infty} = \int_{0}^{\infty}da/(a^{2}\dot a)$ the conformal time from the origin to future infinity (the reading of the dating and of P1: one frozen point, $w = -1$). Write $\eta_{d}$ for the conformal time of the descent and $x_{d} = \eta_{d} - \eta_{\infty}$ for the descent slice in the frozen point's chart.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The pair invariant.)} For points $X = X(x)$, $Y = X(y)$ of the null cone, $Z(X, Y) := 1 + \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}\,\ip{X}{Y}/(\ip{X}{I_{\mathrm{fs}}}\ip{Y}{I_{\mathrm{fs}}})$ is unchanged by rescaling either representative and by every rotor fixing $I_{\mathrm{fs}}$ (the stabiliser $SO(1,4)$ of Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-frozen-point-de-sitter-radius}: spatial rotations, spatial translations, special conformal maps, the dilatation), and it is changed by a time translation. On the chart $Z = 1 - Q(x - y)/(2x_{0}y_{0})$, so at equal time $Z - 1 = |\vec x - \vec y|^{2}/(2x_{0}^{2})$: a two-point function set by the frozen point's global geometry, $G = G(Z)$, depends on the descent slice only through $|\vec x - \vec y|/|x_{d}|$, and its correlations reach the length $|x_{d}|$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Where the descent slice sits, and the range it needs.)} With the record values, $a_{0}H_{0}\eta_{\infty} \in (4.32, 4.34)$ and $a_{0}H_{0}\eta_{0} \in (3.17, 3.19)$; for a descent at $T_{d} \ge 1$ MeV (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-bbn-reheating-temperature-floor}) $a_{0}H_{0}\eta_{d} < 10^{-7}$, so $a_{0}H_{0}|x_{d}| \in (4.32, 4.34)$. The range the stored amplitude bound requires (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-cannot-seed-cmb}(i), (iii), with $\sigma^{2} \le 1$) is one comoving length for every $T_{d}$, $a_{0}H_{0}R_{\mathrm{req}} = (3\pi A_{s}/2)^{1/3}\,a_{0}H_{0}/k_{*} \in (9.4 \times 10^{-6}, 9.8 \times 10^{-6})$ over $A_{s} \in (2.07, 2.13) \times 10^{-9}$ (the stored $460$ and $6.8 \times 10^{17}$ Hubble lengths of the descent are this one length), and $|x_{d}|/R_{\mathrm{req}} > 4.4 \times 10^{5}$. The pivot has $u_{*} := k_{*}|x_{d}| \in (960, 968)$ and the largest observed scales, $k = 2/\eta_{0}$, have $u \in (2.70, 2.74)$: every observed mode is inside the frozen point's Hubble length at the descent (exit is at $u = 1$, in the future, Proposition \claimref{synthesis.finite-range-descent-deposit-cannot-seed-cmb}(iv)). In the other reading of the join, the frozen phase ending at the descent with the scale factor continuous, the same modes sit inside the frozen phase's Hubble length by $k/(a_{d}H_{\Lambda}) > 4 \times 10^{9}$ at $1$ MeV ($> 7 \times 10^{9}$ for $k \ge a_{0}H_{0}$); both readings place every observed mode inside, and nothing below depends on which is taken.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The index of the invariant class.)} Let the deposit on the descent slice be the equal-time two-point function of a state of a scalar field of the series' weight dictionary (Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-frozen-point-dictionary}, $m^{2} = -w(w+3)H^{2}$) on the frozen point's field. For the conformal weight $w = -1$ ($m^{2} = 2H^{2}$) the stabiliser-invariant Hadamard state has $G = H^{2}/(8\pi^{2}(Z - 1)) = 1/(4\pi^{2}a_{\mathrm{fp}}^{2}|\vec x - \vec y|^{2})$ with $a_{\mathrm{fp}} = 1/(H|x_{d}|)$, a correlator homogeneous of degree $-2$ on the slice, so $\Delta^{2}(k) = k^{2}/(4\pi^{2}a_{\mathrm{fp}}^{2})$ and $n_{s} - 1 = 2$ at every $k$. For the massless point $w = 0$ the dilatation-invariant Bunch-Davies state, whose mode $\chi_{k} = e^{-I_4k\eta}(1 - I_4/k\eta)/\sqrt{2k}$ (numbers are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$) solves $\chi'' + (k^{2} - 2/\eta^{2})\chi = 0$, gives $\Delta^{2}(k) = (H/2\pi)^{2}(1 + u^{2})$, $u = k|x_{d}|$, with local index $2u^{2}/(1 + u^{2})$: above $1.99999$ at the pivot and in $(1.7, 1.8)$ at $k = 2/\eta_{0}$. For every other weight with $m^{2} > 0$ the stabiliser-invariant Hadamard state is unique, the Euclidean state, whose mode's Hankel asymptotics give $\Delta^{2} \propto u^{2}(1 + O(u^{-2}))$ at $u \gg |\nu|$; at leading adiabatic order the local index of every field of the unitary series (Fact \claimref{mass.imported-unitary-representations-de-sitter-group}), $3 - u^{2}/(u^{2} + \tfrac14 - \nu^{2})$, lies in $[2 - 2/(u^{2} - 2), 3)$, which at the pivot is above $2 - 3 \times 10^{-6}$ and more than $480$ standard deviations above the measured $n_{s} - 1 = -0.0351 \pm 0.0042$. The $\alpha$-vacua are not Hadamard (an antipodal singularity) and their local index oscillates with amplitude of order $u|\beta_{\alpha}|$: they are excited states whose Bogoliubov coefficient is a datum, not a reading of the frozen point's geometry.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The three classes at the descent.)} On the descent slice a correlator homogeneous of degree $-2\Delta$ gives $n_{s} - 1 = 2\Delta$: finite range (effective degree $-3$ and below) gives $3$ (the stored bound); the frozen point's invariant class gives $2$; a deposit covariant under the slicing's dilatation alone, $G(x_{0}; r) = x_{0}^{-2w}g(r/x_{0})$, has an unconstrained spectrum $\Delta^{2} = F(k|x_{d}|)$ on the slice, the weight fixing the index only as $k|x_{0}| \to 0$, which Proposition \claimref{synthesis.frozen-phase-spectrum-not-red} reads on the far-future boundary. \end{enumerate}
Consequently the frozen point's global geometry supplies the correlation range the measured amplitude needs, with a margin above $4 \times 10^{5}$ at every reheating temperature, and the obstruction to a descent-sourced spectrum is not range but horizon exit: at the descent the observed modes are outside the descent's Hubble length ($k_{*}/a_{d}H_{d} < 5 \times 10^{-6}$ at $1$ MeV) and inside the frozen point's ($k_{*}|x_{d}| > 960$), so a deposit set by the descent's scale is white ($n_{s} - 1 = 3$) and one set by the frozen point's is the vacuum's ($n_{s} - 1 = 2$); the measured index needs a deposited excitation above the vacuum whose occupation numbers nothing in the series fixes. Stationary excitations do not reopen the route: for the states thermal at rapidity period $2\pi c$ on each half of a horizon generator the two-point kernel differs from the vacuum's by $-(c^{-2} - 1)\epsilon^{2}/24 + O(\epsilon^{4})$ at relative separation $\epsilon$ along the generator (filed alongside, synthesis.stationary-horizon-state-is-its-own-edge-scaling-limit), so while $c^{-1}$ is small against $u$ such a state reads as the vacuum, and a member hot enough to resolve the observed modes is a thermal deposit of finite range, the stored bound's class (argued).
synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-de.technical:
The question was whether the series' one global structure before the descent, the frozen point $I$ with its $SO(1,4)$ stabiliser, could correlate the descent's deposit over the lengths the stored finite-range bound demands. It can: the stabiliser's pair invariant $Z$ is a function of the chord $\ip{X}{Y}$ divided by the two scale functions, and on an equal-time slice of the frozen point's flat slicing it reduces to the separation over the slice's conformal distance to future infinity. Placing the descent slice needs one identification, hypothesis (F): the descended universe's late-time de Sitter stage is the frozen point's own field, so the FLRW conformal time runs from the origin to $\eta_{\infty}$ and the descent sits at $x_{0} = -\eta_{\infty}$ in the frozen point's chart. An exact bracket of $\int da/\sqrt{\Omega_{r} + \Omega_{m}a + \Omega_{\Lambda}a^{4}}$ (monotone Riemann sums with integer square roots, record parameters) gives $a_{0}H_{0}\eta_{\infty} \in (4.32, 4.34)$. The required range, once written in comoving units, is independent of the reheating temperature, $a_{0}H_{0}R_{\mathrm{req}} = (3\pi A_{s}/2)^{1/3}/222.4$, about $9.5 \times 10^{-6}$ (the two stored numbers, $460$ at $1$ MeV and $6.8 \times 10^{17}$ at $10^{12}$ GeV, divided by the stored Hubble ratios, both give it); $|x_{d}|$ is $4.4 \times 10^{5}$ times larger.

The index then follows from where the observed modes are relative to the frozen point's horizon: $k|x_{d}|$ runs from $2.7$ at the largest observed scales to about $10^{4}$ at $\ell \approx 2500$, all inside. A state invariant under the stabiliser and Hadamard reads at such separations as the Minkowski vacuum, correlator $1/(4\pi^{2}a^{2}r^{2})$, index $2$; the conformally coupled weight makes this exact at every scale, the massless point's Bunch-Davies spectrum $(H/2\pi)^{2}(1 + u^{2})$ makes the approach to $2$ explicit, and the leading adiabatic index $3 - u^{2}/(u^{2} + \tfrac14 - \nu^{2})$ bounds every unitary-series field between $2 - 2/(u^{2} - 2)$ and $3$ (the leading adiabatic bound, stated here at this matching). The $\alpha$-vacua, not being Hadamard, fall outside the class: their index oscillates and their Bogoliubov coefficient is a datum. This is the counterpart, at the descent, of the stored weight result: that result fixes the index by the dilatation weight only in the limit $k|x_{0}| \to 0$, which for the frozen point of the observed $\Lambda$ is the far future; at the descent dilatation invariance alone leaves the spectrum an arbitrary function of $k|x_{d}|$. The classification is therefore complete for the symmetry classes the series offers: white, vacuum, or unconstrained. The measured spectrum, a correlator growing as $r^{0.035}$, lies on the far side of scale invariance from the vacuum, so it is an excitation deposited mode by mode, in the sense of the quadratic-flows result, with occupation numbers the series does not supply. The join between the frozen phase and the descended phase can also be read with the frozen phase ending at the descent and the scale factor continuous; the observed modes are then inside the frozen horizon by more than $4 \times 10^{9}$ ($7 \times 10^{9}$ for $k \ge a_{0}H_{0}$) and the conclusion is the same. Transport-absent apart from the $\Cl(2,4)$ form; the de Sitter propagators and the Bunch-Davies mode are standard (the mode is verified exactly in the check; that $H^{2}/(8\pi^{2}(Z-1))$ is the invariant Hadamard state of the conformal weight, and the uniqueness of that state for positive mass, are cited from memory).
synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-de.lay: Before the descent there is one global structure in this theory: the frozen point, whose symmetry group is that of de Sitter space. Could that structure have correlated the newborn universe over the enormous distances the cosmic background requires? The arithmetic says yes with a huge margin: the distance it correlates is the present Hubble radius, and the distance the measured amplitude needs is about a hundred-thousandth of that. But the same arithmetic says what spectrum such a correlation would give. At the descent every scale we now observe was deep inside the frozen point's horizon, and a de Sitter-symmetric state looks there like empty flat space, whose ripples grow steeply with wavenumber (index $2$ above scale invariance) rather than falling gently (the measured $0.035$ below it). So the frozen point can supply the reach of the correlations but not their shape; the shape would have to be an excitation the descent deposits, and nothing in the theory yet says what it is.

synthesis.hadamard-condition-leaves-the-.formal:
Let $\phi$ be a real scalar field on a spatially flat Robertson-Walker field in conformal time, $\chi = a\phi$, and let $\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}$ be a homogeneous isotropic quasi-free Hadamard state with mode functions $\chi_{k}(\eta)$ (smooth in $\eta$, continuous in $k > 0$, Wronskian $\chi_{k}\bar\chi_{k}' - \chi_{k}'\bar\chi_{k} = I_{4}$) and slice spectrum $\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}(k) = k^{3}|\chi_{k}(\eta_{d})|^{2}/(2\pi^{2}a^{2})$ on a slice $\eta = \eta_{d}$. A homogeneous isotropic quasi-free state $\omega$ is given relative to $\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}$ by measurable data $n_{k} \ge 0$, $c_{k}$ with $|c_{k}|^{2} \le n_{k}(n_{k} + 1)$ ($n_{k} = |\beta_{k}|^{2}$, $c_{k} = \alpha_{k}\bar\beta_{k}$ for a pure state with modes $u_{k} = \alpha_{k}\chi_{k} + \beta_{k}\bar\chi_{k}$, $|\alpha_{k}|^{2} - |\beta_{k}|^{2} = 1$); its slice spectrum is $\Delta_{\omega}^{2} = \rho_{k}\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}$ with $\rho_{k} = 1 + 2n_{k} + 2\,\mathrm{Re}(c_{k}\theta_{k})$, $\theta_{k} = \chi_{k}(\eta_{d})^{2}/|\chi_{k}(\eta_{d})|^{2}$. Complex numbers are read as $a + bI_{4}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Bands are free.)} If $n_{k}$ and $c_{k}$ are bounded and vanish outside a bounded shell $k_{1} \le k \le k_{2}$, $k_{1} > 0$, then $\omega$ is Hadamard: its two-point function differs from that of $\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}$ by a smooth bisolution. For every continuous $\rho: [k_{1}, k_{2}] \to (0, \infty)$ the pure state with $|\beta_{k}| = \sinh(|\ln\rho_{k}|/2)$, $\beta_{k}\bar\theta_{k}$ in phase with $\alpha_{k}$ for $\rho_{k} \ge 1$ and opposite in phase for $\rho_{k} < 1$, and $\beta_{k} = 0$ off the band, is such a state and has slice spectrum $\rho_{k}\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}$ on the band and $\Delta_{\mathrm{ref}}^{2}$ off it. So the amplitude and the index of the spectrum on any bounded band are not constrained by the Hadamard condition.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The price of a ratio.)} Every $\omega$ has $4n_{k}\rho_{k} \ge (\rho_{k} - 1)^{2}$, that is $n_{k} \ge (\sqrt{\rho_{k}} - 1/\sqrt{\rho_{k}})^{2}/4$, with equality for the pure states of (i).
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The ultraviolet end, conformally coupled field.)} Let $\phi$ be conformally coupled and massless, so $\chi'' + k^{2}\chi = 0$, and let $\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}$ be its conformal vacuum, $\chi_{k} = e^{-I_{4}k\eta}/\sqrt{2k}$, assumed Hadamard (on the frozen point's field, $a = -1/(H\eta)$, this is the field of weight $w = -1$ of the dictionary of Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-frozen-point-dictionary}, $m^{2} = 2H^{2}$, and its conformal vacuum is the stabiliser-invariant Hadamard state of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-de-sitter-invariant-hadamard-state-unique} used in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-descent-as-vacuum}, slice spectrum $k^{2}/(4\pi^{2}a^{2})$). If $\omega$ is Hadamard then $\int k^{3 + 2j}n_{k}\,dk < \infty$ for every integer $j \ge 0$. Hence no law $\rho_{k} = Ck^{q}$ with $(C, q) \neq (1, 0)$ holds for all $k$ above any $K$ in a Hadamard state: no power-law ratio on a band unbounded toward short scales; in particular a slice correlator homogeneous of degree $-2\Delta$ with $\Delta \neq 1$ is not the slice two-point function of a Hadamard state, and the occupation law $n_{k} \propto k^{n_{s} - 3}$ cannot hold up to arbitrarily large $k$. A homogeneous isotropic quasi-free Hadamard state invariant under the dilatation $(\eta, \vec x) \mapsto (\lambda\eta, \lambda\vec x)$ of the frozen point's field is $\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The infrared end, for slice fields of nonzero mean.)} The slice fields $\phi(g)$ have finite variance in $\omega$ for every test function $g$, those of nonzero mean included, only if $\int_{0}^{k_{1}}\Delta_{\omega}^{2}(k)\,dk/k < \infty$. A law $\Delta_{\omega}^{2} \propto k^{n - 1}$ with $n \le 1$ (red or scale invariant) on an interval $(0, k_{1})$ fails this; blue laws ($n > 1$) on $(0, k_{1})$ meet it, and so may be Hadamard there. The Hadamard condition does not involve this integral.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, if the deposited state is Hadamard, a red spectrum is allowed on any bounded band, on no band unbounded toward short scales and, for slice fields of nonzero mean, on no band reaching $k = 0$: it must end below some $k_{\mathrm{IR}} > 0$ and above some $k_{\mathrm{UV}} < \infty$, and neither end, nor the amplitude and index between them, is fixed by the Hadamard condition.
synthesis.hadamard-condition-leaves-the-.technical:
The question is what the Hadamard condition would say about the primordial spectrum if the descent's deposit satisfied it. The answer is: nothing on any bounded band of scales. Measured against any homogeneous Hadamard reference state (on the frozen point's field, its invariant state; on a collar of the descent, an admissible vacuum there), a deposit is described by occupations $n_{k}$ and pair terms $c_{k}$; if these vanish outside a bounded shell, the deposit differs from the reference by a smooth kernel and is Hadamard. Every positive ratio to the reference spectrum on a band is reached by a squeezed pure state, at the price $n_{k} \ge (\sqrt{\rho} - 1/\sqrt{\rho})^{2}/4$. So the amplitude and the tilt on the observed band are free data.

The condition bites only toward short scales. For the conformally coupled field the energy difference has the positive Fourier weight $2kn_{k}$ exactly, with no cross term, so a Hadamard state has finite moments $\int k^{3 + 2j}n_{k}\,dk$: no power-law ratio continues to arbitrarily short scales, and a dilatation-invariant homogeneous Hadamard state is the vacuum, of index $2$. At long scales the state has to exist on slice fields of nonzero mean: their variance needs $\int_{0}\Delta^{2}\,dk/k < \infty$, which a red or scale-invariant law continued to $k \to 0$ violates, while a blue law there is allowed. A red band therefore needs an ultraviolet and an infrared end. The ingredients (finite-band Bogoliubov data, rapid decay of occupations, the infrared divergence of Ford and Parker, the uniqueness of the invariant state) are standard; the reading for the deposit is the content. The result is transport-absent.
synthesis.hadamard-condition-leaves-the-.lay: The series needs the quantum state left by the descent to be of a regular kind, called Hadamard, so that energies and horizon physics make sense. One might hope that this regularity would also fix the pattern of primordial ripples seen in the sky. This result shows it does not. The Hadamard condition only controls the shortest distances; over any finite range of scales, including the whole range astronomers measure, the state can have any strength and any tilt of ripples. What the condition and the existence of the state do require is that a pattern tilted like the observed one must stop somewhere at very short scales and somewhere at very long ones, and nothing in the condition says where.

proofs.main:
\emph{Scope.} Clauses (i), (ii) and (iv) use only the mode functions $\chi_{k}$ of a homogeneous Hadamard reference state $\omega_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (smooth in $\eta$, continuous in $k > 0$) and the smooth-difference characterisation of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}: the wave front set condition of part (a), with part (b)'s statement that two Hadamard states differ by a smooth kernel. Below they are written for the checked instance, the conformal vacuum $\omega_{0}$ on the frozen point's field, with $e^{-2I_{4}k\eta_{d}}$ in place of the general phase $\theta_{k} = \chi_{k}(\eta_{d})^{2}/|\chi_{k}(\eta_{d})|^{2}$; for a general reference replace $e^{-I_{4}k\eta}/\sqrt{2k}$ by $\chi_{k}$ throughout, and the bound on the integrand in (i) by the supremum of $|\chi_{k}|$ and its $\eta$-derivatives over the compact shell and a compact time interval. Clause (iii) uses the conformal modes; on a spatially flat Robertson-Walker field other than the frozen point's, the conformal vacuum of the conformally coupled field is the flat vacuum of $\chi = a\phi$ by the conformal covariance of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-conformal-covariance-of-massless-fields-and-local-conformal-flatness}(b), and that it is Hadamard there is the assumption stated in (iii). These ingredients are standard (finite-band Bogoliubov data, rapid decay of the occupations of a Hadamard state, Ford and Parker's infrared divergence, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-ford-parker-infrared-divergence}, the alpha-vacua); the scalar necessity argument of (iii) is the counterpart of the occupation-moment criterion for the massless Dirac field (\claimref{synthesis.deposit-over-the-conformal-vacuum-is-hadamard-exactly-when-every-occupation-moment-is-finite}).

\emph{Setting.} On the frozen point's field in its flat slicing, $a = -1/(H\eta)$ and $a''/a = 2/\eta^{2}$. A scalar of weight $w$ in the dictionary of Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-frozen-point-dictionary} has $m^{2} = -w(w + 3)H^{2}$, and $\chi = a\phi$ obeys $\chi'' + (k^{2} + m^{2}a^{2} - a''/a)\chi = 0$. For $w = -1$, $m^{2}a^{2} = 2H^{2}/(H^{2}\eta^{2}) = 2/\eta^{2}$ cancels $a''/a$ exactly, so $\chi'' + k^{2}\chi = 0$ (for the massless point $w = 0$ the term $-2/\eta^{2}$ stays; the check verifies both). The solutions $\chi_{k} = e^{-I_{4}k\eta}/\sqrt{2k}$ have Wronskian $\chi_{k}\bar\chi_{k}' - \chi_{k}'\bar\chi_{k} = I_{4}$. The state with these modes is invariant under the stabiliser of the frozen point and is Hadamard; by Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-de-sitter-invariant-hadamard-state-unique} ($m^{2} = 2H^{2} > 0$) it is the unique such state, the one used in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-descent-as-vacuum}(iii), whose slice spectrum is $\Delta_{0}^{2} = k^{3}|\chi_{k}|^{2}/(2\pi^{2}a^{2}) = k^{2}/(4\pi^{2}a^{2})$. The complex unit of the mode functions is $I_{4}$, $I_{4}^{2} = -1$; the check verifies that the product of numbers $a + bI_{4}$ in the spacetime algebra is the complex product it uses.

A homogeneous isotropic quasi-free state $\omega$ has, in the Fock modes $a_{\vec k}$ of $\omega_{0}$, $\omega(a_{\vec k}^{*}a_{\vec k'}) = n_{k}\delta(\vec k - \vec k')$ and $\omega(a_{\vec k}a_{-\vec k'}) = c_{k}\delta(\vec k - \vec k')$; positivity of the two-mode covariance requires $n_{k} \ge 0$ and $|c_{k}|^{2} \le n_{k}(n_{k} + 1)$, with equality exactly for pure states, where $n_{k} = |\beta_{k}|^{2}$ and $c_{k} = \alpha_{k}\bar\beta_{k}$ up to the phase convention. The symmetrised equal-time two-point function of $\chi$ at $\eta_{d}$ then has Fourier weight $|\chi_{k}|^{2}(1 + 2n_{k}) + 2\,\mathrm{Re}(c_{k}\chi_{k}(\eta_{d})^{2})$, which is $|\chi_{k}|^{2}\rho_{k}$ with $\rho_{k} = 1 + 2n_{k} + 2\,\mathrm{Re}(c_{k}e^{-2I_{4}k\eta_{d}})$. For a pure state this is $|u_{k}|^{2} = |\chi_{k}|^{2}|\alpha_{k} + \beta_{k}e^{2I_{4}k\eta_{d}}|^{2}$.

\emph{(i)} Write the two-point function of $\omega$ minus that of $\omega_{0}$ as the mode integral
\[
D(x, y) = \frac{1}{a(\eta)a(\eta')}\int_{k_{1} \le |\vec k| \le k_{2}}\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\Bigl[2n_{k}\,\mathrm{Re}\bigl(\chi_{k}(\eta)\bar\chi_{k}(\eta')\bigr)\cos(\vec k\cdot(\vec x - \vec y)) + \bigl(c_{k}\chi_{k}(\eta)\chi_{k}(\eta') + \text{c.c.}\bigr)\cos(\vec k\cdot(\vec x - \vec y))\Bigr]
\]
(the antisymmetric part, the commutator, is state-independent). The integrand is bounded by $(2\sup n + 2\sup|c|)/(2k_{1})$ on a compact set of $\vec k$, it is smooth in $(\eta, \eta', \vec x, \vec y)$, and each derivative of order $N$ multiplies it by at most $k_{2}^{N}$; so differentiation under the integral is allowed to every order and $D$ is $C^{\infty}$ (indeed real-analytic). It is a bisolution, being a superposition of products of solutions. By Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(a) the Hadamard property is the wave front set condition on the two-point distribution, and adding a smooth kernel does not change a wave front set; $\omega_{0}$ satisfies the condition, hence so does $\omega$. The check computes an instance: for $n_{k} = n$ constant and $c_{k} = 0$ on $[k_{1}, k_{2}]$ the equal-time difference is $n(\cos k_{1}r - \cos k_{2}r)/(2\pi^{2}a^{2}r^{2})$, from $\int_{k_{1}}^{k_{2}}k\,\sin(kr)/(kr)\,dk = (\cos k_{1}r - \cos k_{2}r)/r^{2}$, whose Taylor series in $r^{2}$ it verifies term by term against the term-by-term integral to order $r^{22}$; its value at $r = 0$ is $n(k_{2}^{2} - k_{1}^{2})/(4\pi^{2}a^{2})$, while $\omega_{0}$'s equal-time kernel is $1/(4\pi^{2}a^{2}r^{2})$.

For the realisation of a ratio, put $q_{k} = \sqrt{\rho_{k}}$, $\alpha_{k} = (q_{k} + 1/q_{k})/2 = \cosh s_{k}$ and $\beta_{k} = \pm\frac12(q_{k} - 1/q_{k})e^{-2I_{4}k\eta_{d}}$, so $|\beta_{k}| = \sinh|s_{k}|$ with $s_{k} = \ln q_{k}$ and $|\alpha_{k}|^{2} - |\beta_{k}|^{2} = 1$. With the upper sign $|\alpha_{k} + \beta_{k}e^{2I_{4}k\eta_{d}}|^{2} = (\cosh s_{k} + \sinh s_{k})^{2} = q_{k}^{2} = \rho_{k}$, with the lower sign $(\cosh s_{k} - \sinh s_{k})^{2} = 1/q_{k}^{2}$; choosing the sign by whether $\rho_{k} \ge 1$ (and using $|\sinh|$) gives the stated state. The coefficients are bounded on the band because $\rho$ is continuous and positive on a compact interval, and set to zero off it, so the first part applies. The check verifies, with exact Gaussian rationals and $2k$ a rational square, that for nine values of $q$ (from $1/3$ to $1000$), both signs, four values of $k$ and six points $e^{-I_{4}k\eta_{d}}$ of the unit circle, the new modes keep the Wronskian $I_{4}$, $|\beta|^{2} = ((q - 1/q)/2)^{2}$, and $|u_{k}|^{2}/|\chi_{k}|^{2}$ equals $q^{2}$ or $1/q^{2}$ exactly. Since the ratio is arbitrary, so are the amplitude and the local index $d\ln\Delta_{\omega}^{2}/d\ln k = 2 + d\ln\rho_{k}/d\ln k$ on the band.

\emph{(ii)} Write $t = 2\,\mathrm{Re}(c_{k}e^{-2I_{4}k\eta_{d}})$, so $\rho = 1 + 2n + t$ and $t^{2} \le 4|c|^{2} \le 4n(n + 1)$. Then $(\rho - 1)^{2} - 4n\rho = (2n + t)^{2} - 4n(1 + 2n + t) = t^{2} - 4n^{2} - 4n \le 0$. Equality holds when $t^{2} = 4n(n + 1)$, which the states of (i) attain ($n = \sinh^{2}s$, $|c| = \sinh|s|\cosh s$, phase aligned or opposed). Solving the quadratic, $4n \ge \rho + 1/\rho - 2 = (\sqrt\rho - 1/\sqrt\rho)^{2}$. The check tests the inequality at every admissible sample of $n$ (five values), $c$ (twenty values, those with $|c|^{2} \le n(n + 1)$ kept) and six phases, and the equality for the pure data.

\emph{(iii)} Let $\omega$ be Hadamard. By part (b) of the Fact (the two-point functions of two Hadamard states differ by a smooth kernel; for the Klein-Gordon field this follows from part (a), both two-point distributions having the wave front set $C^{+}$ and the same antisymmetric part) $D$ is smooth. Apply $\partial_{\eta}\partial_{\eta'} + \nabla_{\vec x}\cdot\nabla_{\vec y}$ to $a(\eta)a(\eta')D$ and set $\eta = \eta'$: the result $e(\vec x - \vec y)$ is a smooth function of the separation. Its Fourier weight is $(|u_{k}'|^{2} + k^{2}|u_{k}|^{2}) - (|\chi_{k}'|^{2} + k^{2}|\chi_{k}|^{2})$ for pure states and, in general, $2n_{k}(|\chi_{k}'|^{2} + k^{2}|\chi_{k}|^{2}) + 2\,\mathrm{Re}\bigl(c_{k}(\chi_{k}'^{2} + k^{2}\chi_{k}^{2})\bigr)$. For the conformal modes $\chi_{k}'^{2} + k^{2}\chi_{k}^{2} = (-k^{2} + k^{2})\chi_{k}^{2} = 0$ exactly and $|\chi_{k}'|^{2} + k^{2}|\chi_{k}|^{2} = k$, so the weight is $2kn_{k} \ge 0$ with no cross term (the check verifies $|u'|^{2} + k^{2}|u|^{2} = k(|\alpha|^{2} + |\beta|^{2})$ for three pairs at every sample, and, as a control, that the massless point's Bunch-Davies mode $e^{-I_{4}z}(1 - I_{4}/z)$ has $\chi'^{2} + k^{2}\chi^{2} = \tfrac{k}{2}(2/z^{2} - 2I_{4}/z^{3} - 1/z^{4})e^{-2I_{4}z} \neq 0$). A function continuous at $0$ whose Fourier transform is a nonnegative function has that transform integrable, with integral the value at $0$ (smear with a normalised Gaussian of width $\epsilon$ and let $\epsilon \to 0$: the left side tends to $e(0)$, the right side increases to $\int 2kn_{k}\,d^{3}k/(2\pi)^{3}$ by monotone convergence). So $\int k^{3}n_{k}\,dk < \infty$. Applying the Laplacian $j$ times before setting the arguments equal multiplies the weight by $k^{2j}$ and gives $\int k^{3 + 2j}n_{k}\,dk < \infty$.

If $\rho_{k} = Ck^{q}$ for $k \ge K$, (ii) gives $4n_{k} \ge Ck^{q} + C^{-1}k^{-q} - 2$, which grows like $k^{|q|}$ for $q \neq 0$ and is the positive constant $C + C^{-1} - 2$ for $q = 0$, $C \neq 1$; in both cases $\int^{\infty}k^{3}n_{k}\,dk$ diverges, so $\omega$ is not Hadamard. The check computes exact lower bounds of $\int k^{3}n_{k}\,dk$ over the shells $[b^{j}, b^{j+1}]$, $b = 2^{10000}$, $j = 1, 2, 3$, for $q = -20351/10000$ (the law $n_{k} \propto k^{n_{s} - 3}$ at the stored central $n_{s} = 0.9649$, used only as a sample exponent), $q = -1$ and $q = 1/2$, and finds each above $1$ and increasing. A slice correlator homogeneous of degree $-2\Delta$ has $\Delta^{2} \propto k^{2\Delta}$ at every $k$ (the scaling lemma of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-descent-as-vacuum}(iv)), so $\rho_{k} \propto k^{2\Delta - 2}$, excluded for $\Delta \neq 1$. The frozen point's dilatation $(\eta, \vec x) \mapsto (\lambda\eta, \lambda\vec x)$ fixes $\omega_{0}$ and acts on the modes by $\vec k \mapsto \vec k/\lambda$ with $k\eta$ fixed, so a dilatation-invariant $\omega$ has $n_{k}$ and $c_{k}$ constant on $k > 0$; then $\int k^{3}n\,dk < \infty$ forces $n = 0$, hence $c = 0$ and $\omega = \omega_{0}$ (the check shows the shell bounds of a constant occupation grow by more than a factor $15$ per shell of ratio $16$).

\emph{(iv)} For a test function $g$ on the slice, $\omega(\phi(g)^{2}) = \int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}|\hat g(\vec k)|^{2}\frac{2\pi^{2}}{k^{3}}\Delta_{\omega}^{2}(k) = \int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{k}\Delta_{\omega}^{2}(k)\,\langle|\hat g|^{2}\rangle_{k}$, with $\langle|\hat g|^{2}\rangle_{k}$ the angular mean. Since $\hat g$ is continuous with $\hat g(0) = \int g$, for every $g$ of nonzero mean $\langle|\hat g|^{2}\rangle_{k} \ge \tfrac12|\int g|^{2}$ on some $(0, \delta)$, so finiteness for all $g$ needs $\int_{0}\Delta_{\omega}^{2}\,dk/k < \infty$. For $\Delta_{\omega}^{2} = Ck^{n - 1}$ on $(0, k_{1})$ the integral is $C\int_{0}^{k_{1}}k^{n - 2}\,dk$, divergent for $n \le 1$; for $\omega_{0}$, $\int_{0}k\,dk$ converges. The condition excludes only $n \le 1$ near $k = 0$: for instance $\rho_{k} = 1/k$ on $(0, 1]$ (slice index $2$) is realised by the pure states of (i) with $n_{k} = (1 - k)^{2}/(4k)$, $|c_{k}| = (1 - k^{2})/(4k)$; then $\int_{0}^{1}kn_{k}\,dk = 1/12$ and $\int_{0}^{1}k|c_{k}|\,dk = 1/6$, so the difference kernel is smooth (derivatives add bounded powers of $k$ on a bounded set), the state is Hadamard, and $\int_{0}\Delta_{\omega}^{2}\,dk/k$ converges: a power law on a band reaching $k = 0$ is allowed when it is blue enough, so the infrared clause concerns red and scale-invariant laws only. The check evaluates $\int_{\epsilon}^{1}k^{s - 1}\,dk = (1 - \epsilon^{s})/s$ exactly at $\epsilon = 2^{-10000m}$ for $s = -351/10000$ (values $(2^{351m} - 1)\cdot 10000/351$, unbounded), sums forty dyadic shells for $s = 0$ (total $20$, each $\tfrac12$), and bounds the vacuum's $s = 2$ by $\tfrac12$. The Hadamard condition (i) and (iii) involves only the behaviour of $n_{k}$ and $c_{k}$ as $k \to \infty$, so it does not decide this integral.

\emph{Conclusion.} By (i) any bounded band can carry any positive spectrum in a Hadamard state; by (iii) a red (or any power-law) ratio has to stop at some finite $k_{\mathrm{UV}}$; by (iv) a red law has to stop at some $k_{\mathrm{IR}} > 0$ for the state to exist on the slice fields of nonzero mean, while a blue law may continue to $k = 0$. Neither (i) nor (iii) nor (iv) gives a value of $k_{\mathrm{UV}}$, $k_{\mathrm{IR}}$, the amplitude or the index on the band.

synthesis.holographic-thermal-fluctuatio.formal:
Assume the conversion of thermal fluctuations at Hubble exit used in string-gas cosmology (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-string-gas-thermal-spectrum-and-conversion}): a mode of physical wavenumber $k$ that leaves the Hubble length from a thermal phase of temperature $T$ carries $P_{\Phi}(k) = 8G^{2}k^{-4}\langle\delta\rho^{2}\rangle_{R}$ with $\langle\delta\rho^{2}\rangle_{R} = T^{2}C(R)/R^{6}$ at $R = 1/k$, where $C(R)$ is the heat capacity of a region of size $R$, and $\Phi = \tfrac23\zeta$ in the radiation era after exit (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-large-scale-potential-and-sachs-wolfe-relations}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Index.)} If $C \propto R^{\gamma}$ and the temperature at exit varies as $T \propto R^{\tau}$ across the exiting scales, then $P_{\Phi} \propto k^{2 - \gamma - 2\tau}$, so $n_{s} - 1 = 2 - \gamma - 2\tau$. The area law, $\gamma = 2$ (Proposition \claimref{singularity.area-law-test} for horizons), at fixed temperature gives $n_{s} = 1$ exactly, between $8.3$ and $8.4$ standard deviations from the measured $n_{s} - 1 = -0.0351 \pm 0.0042$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}); an extensive capacity gives $-1$; the area law at a modular temperature $T \propto 1/R$ gives $+2$. The measured value needs $\gamma + 2\tau = 2.0351$: with the area law, a temperature at exit rising as $R^{0.01755}$, one exponent for one number.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Amplitude.)} With $C = \lambda A/4G$, $A = 4\pi R^{2}$, $P_{\Phi} = 8\pi\lambda (T/M_{\mathrm{Pl}})^{2}$ for every $k$. If the temperature at exit is at most the ceiling $7.3 \times 10^{8}$ GeV of the descent's window (Proposition \claimref{synthesis.untuned-fit-caps-lightest-heavy-neutrino}, under Premise (R)), then $P_{\Phi} < 9.0 \times 10^{-20}\lambda$, short of $\tfrac49 A_{s} = 9.33 \times 10^{-10}$ by more than $10^{10}$ unless $\lambda > 10^{10}$; at $\lambda = 1$ the measured amplitude needs $7.4 \times 10^{13} < T < 7.5 \times 10^{13}$ GeV, above the ceiling by more than $10^{5}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Frozen point.)} At the frozen point's Gibbons-Hawking temperature $T = H_{\Lambda}/2\pi$, $H_{\Lambda}^{2} = H_{0}^{2}\Omega_{\Lambda}$ (the frozen phase of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-descent-as-vacuum} under hypothesis (F)), $P_{\Phi} = 2\lambda H_{0}^{2}\Omega_{\Lambda}/(\pi M_{\mathrm{Pl}}^{2})$ lies between $10^{-123}\lambda$ and $10^{-122}\lambda$, short by more than $10^{112}$.
\end{enumerate}
So with the series' area law and either of its temperatures, the thermal-holographic mechanism gives the measured amplitude only with a heat capacity about $10^{10}$ times the area entropy or more, and its index only with a fitted temperature exponent.
synthesis.holographic-thermal-fluctuatio.technical:
String-gas cosmology replaces inflation's quantum fluctuations with thermal ones: in a quasi-static hot phase, a region of size $R$ has energy fluctuations set by its heat capacity, and if that capacity grows like the area of the region rather than its volume, the curvature perturbation left when the region leaves the Hubble length is the same on every scale. The series has two ingredients that resemble this: an area law for horizon entropy (not a heat capacity of sub-horizon regions, which the mechanism assumes), and a join at which the observed modes go from inside the frozen phase's horizon to outside the descent's Hubble length, the same sudden exit the string gas uses. Taking the cited conversion at face value, simple power counting gives the index as $2 - \gamma - 2\tau$ for capacity $\propto R^{\gamma}$ and temperature $\propto R^{\tau}$: the area law at fixed temperature is exactly scale invariant, over eight standard deviations from the measured red tilt, and the tilt needs a temperature exponent of about $0.018$ that nothing fixes. The amplitude is $8\pi\lambda(T/M_{\mathrm{Pl}})^{2}$ for a capacity of $\lambda$ times the area entropy. At the descent window's ceiling under Premise (R), $7.3 \times 10^{8}$ GeV, it is below $9 \times 10^{-20}\lambda$, about ten orders short; the measured amplitude needs about $7.4 \times 10^{13}$ GeV at $\lambda = 1$. At the frozen point's horizon temperature it is about $10^{-122}$. The string gas reaches the needed amplitude through a capacity enhanced near its Hagedorn temperature; the series has no limiting temperature, so the route needs an input the series does not supply.

\emph{Note (the conversion and the descent slice; added 16 November).} The conversion taken from the string-gas Fact is the Poisson relation with the potential read as the growing solution's: in the terms of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.descent-slice-constraints-and-the-three-readings-of-a-white-deposit} it is the reading (UE), a descent slice of uniform expansion, up to the factor between $\Phi$ and $\tfrac23\zeta$ (the variant (UE$_{\Phi}$) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.quasi-free-deposit-has-white-energy-noise-unless-pure-and-stationary}). It is a hypothesis of this result, as the statement says; the series leaves the slice's expansion datum free and adopts no reading. An extensive capacity is white energy noise: its index $-1$ here and the index $3$ of clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.quasi-free-deposit-is-vacuum-plus-shot-noise}, which is stated there under the flat-slice reading (FR), are the same white noise read through different slice data. The amplitudes of (ii) and (iii) are amplitudes under this conversion.
synthesis.holographic-thermal-fluctuatio.lay: One alternative to a rapid early expansion seeds the early universe's ripples with heat: in a hot early phase, regions of different sizes have random energy differences, and if the heat a region can hold grows only with its surface area, the ripples come out the same on every scale. This framework has an area law for horizon entropy, though not the heat capacity the mechanism needs, and a moment when the ripples are carried out of causal contact. But with the framework's own numbers, the ripples come out exactly equal on all scales, where a slight tilt is measured, and, if a region holds no more heat than its surface-area entropy allows and the temperature is one the framework allows, they are about ten billion times too weak or worse.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} At $R = 1/k$, $\langle\delta\rho^{2}\rangle_{R} = T^{2}C/R^{6} \propto R^{2\tau + \gamma - 6} = k^{6 - \gamma - 2\tau}$, so $P_{\Phi} = 8G^{2}k^{-4}\langle\delta\rho^{2}\rangle_{R}$ (the conversion of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-string-gas-thermal-spectrum-and-conversion}) $\propto k^{2 - \gamma - 2\tau}$. Since $P_{\Phi}$ is the dimensionless spectrum and $\Phi = \tfrac23\zeta$ is fixed outside the Hubble length in the radiation era (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-large-scale-potential-and-sachs-wolfe-relations}), the index of $\zeta$ is $n_{s} - 1 = 2 - \gamma - 2\tau$. The cases: $(\gamma, \tau) = (2, 0)$ gives $0$; $(3, 0)$ gives $-1$; $(2, -1)$ gives $2$. Against $n_{s} - 1 = -0.0351 \pm 0.0042$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-planck-2018-lcdm-parameters}), $0.0351/0.0042 = 8.357$. Solving $2 - \gamma - 2\tau = -0.0351$ gives $\gamma + 2\tau = 2.0351$, and at $\gamma = 2$, $\tau = 0.01755$. The area-law exponent $\gamma = 2$ is the scaling of the horizon entropy with area in Proposition \claimref{singularity.area-law-test}; its use for a heat capacity of a sub-horizon region is the hypothesis of the mechanism, not a result of the series.

\emph{(ii)} With $C = \lambda A/4G = \lambda\pi R^{2}/G$, $P_{\Phi} = 8G^{2}k^{-4}T^{2}\lambda\pi R^{2}/(GR^{6}) = 8\pi\lambda G T^{2}$ at $R = 1/k$, independent of $k$, with $G = 1/M_{\mathrm{Pl}}^{2}$. With $3.14159 < \pi < 3.1416$ and $M_{\mathrm{Pl}} = 1.22089 \times 10^{19}$ GeV, at $T = 7.3 \times 10^{8}$ GeV, the ceiling of the window for the descent's reheating temperature under Premise (R) set by Proposition \claimref{synthesis.untuned-fit-caps-lightest-heavy-neutrino}, $8.9 \times 10^{-20} < P_{\Phi}/\lambda < 9.0 \times 10^{-20}$. The target is $\tfrac49 A_{s} = \tfrac{14}{15} \times 10^{-9}$; the ratio exceeds $1.0 \times 10^{10}$. Solving $8\pi T^{2}/M_{\mathrm{Pl}}^{2} = \tfrac49 A_{s}$ gives $T^{2}$ between $(7.4 \times 10^{13})^{2}$ and $(7.5 \times 10^{13})^{2}$ GeV$^{2}$, above $(10^{5} \times 7.3 \times 10^{8})^{2}$. At the nucleosynthesis floor $T = 1$ MeV, $P_{\Phi} < 10^{-42}\lambda$.

\emph{(iii)} The frozen phase of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-geometry-reads-descent-as-vacuum} is de Sitter with $H_{\Lambda}^{2} = \Lambda/3 = H_{0}^{2}\Omega_{\Lambda}$ under hypothesis (F); its horizon temperature is $H_{\Lambda}/2\pi$. Then $P_{\Phi} = 8\pi\lambda H_{\Lambda}^{2}/(4\pi^{2}M_{\mathrm{Pl}}^{2}) = 2\lambda H_{0}^{2}\Omega_{\Lambda}/(\pi M_{\mathrm{Pl}}^{2})$. With $H_{0} = 67.36$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, $1$ Mpc $= 3.08568 \times 10^{19}$ km and $\hbar = 6.58212 \times 10^{-25}$ GeV s, $1.436 \times 10^{-42} < H_{0} < 1.438 \times 10^{-42}$ GeV; $\Omega_{\Lambda} = 1 - 0.3153 - 0.000092 = 0.684608$; so $10^{-123} < P_{\Phi}/\lambda < 10^{-122}$, and the target exceeds it by more than $10^{112}$. The check verifies every inequality in exact rational arithmetic.

synthesis.imported-bbn-reheating-tempera.formal: If the radiation-dominated universe is produced by the decay of a massive particle, of mass between $10$ GeV and $100$ TeV, into Standard-Model radiation at reheating temperature $T_{\mathrm{RH}}$, then consistency of the predicted light-element abundances with the observed ones, with the thermalisation of the oscillating, self-interacting neutrinos computed, requires $T_{\mathrm{RH}} \gtrsim 1.8$ MeV when the decay is radiative and $T_{\mathrm{RH}} \gtrsim 4$ to $5$ MeV when it is hadronic (conservative bounds). In particular any epoch of radiation domination from which nucleosynthesis proceeds in the standard way begins at a temperature above $1$ MeV. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Hasegawa2019} (abstract and main results).
synthesis.imported-bbn-reheating-tempera.technical: Nucleosynthesis needs a thermal bath of photons, electrons and three nearly thermal neutrino species at temperatures of about one MeV. If that bath was produced late, by the decay of a long-lived particle, the neutrinos may not reach thermal equilibrium, which changes the neutron-proton ratio and the expansion rate and spoils the light-element abundances. Requiring the abundances to agree with observation gives a lower bound on the reheating temperature of a few MeV, at least $1.8$ MeV for radiative and $4$ to $5$ MeV for hadronic decays. The store uses the weaker statement that the descended phase's radiation era starts above $1$ MeV.
synthesis.imported-bbn-reheating-tempera.lay: The lightest chemical elements were made in the first few minutes, and the amounts observed today only come out right if the universe was already hot and filled with radiation, including neutrinos, at temperatures of a few million electronvolts. So whatever started the hot universe must have done so above that temperature.

synthesis.imported-bessel-reduction-and-.technical: A wave equation with a time-dependent friction term and a frequency that grows as a power of time reduces to Bessel's equation after a change of variable; the order of the Bessel function is the ratio of the friction exponent to the frequency exponent. The Hankel functions describe the mode that starts in its vacuum, and their behaviour at small argument, a power set by the order, gives the spectrum of the mode after it has stopped oscillating.
synthesis.imported-bessel-reduction-and-.lay: These are textbook properties of Bessel functions, the standard functions that describe waves whose medium changes as a power of time. They are what turns the equations for field fluctuations near a Kasner singularity into a definite tilt of the spectrum.

imported_from.citation: F. W. J. Olver et al. (eds.), NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, Release 1.2.

synthesis.imported-curvaton-and-modulate.formal:
For a curvaton $\sigma$ with quadratic potential that dominates the energy density when it decays ($R = 1$) and decays instantly, the curvature perturbation after the decay is a local function of the curvaton's fractional fluctuation $X = \delta\sigma_{*}/\sigma_{*}$ at horizon exit:
\[
\zeta_{\sigma} = \tfrac23 X - \tfrac13 X^{2} + \tfrac29 X^{3} + \cdots.
\]
For modulated reheating, an inflaton decaying while it oscillates at a rate $\Gamma_{\phi}(\sigma)$ set by a light field, with $\Gamma_{\phi}/m_{\phi}$ small, the generated curvature perturbation is $Q \simeq -\tfrac16\log(\Gamma_{\phi}(\sigma)/H_{c})$, so at first order $\zeta = Q_{\sigma}\,\delta\sigma$ with $Q_{\sigma} = -\tfrac16\,\partial_{\sigma}\Gamma_{\phi}/\Gamma_{\phi}$, that is $\zeta = -\tfrac16\,\delta\Gamma/\Gamma$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{ChoiSeto2012} (eqs. (16), (45), (46)).
synthesis.imported-curvaton-and-modulate.technical: In the curvaton and modulated-reheating mechanisms the curvature perturbation is not made by the field that drives the expansion but converted, at a decay, from the fluctuation of a light spectator: in the first through the spectator's own energy density at its decay, in the second through a decay rate that depends on it. Either way the curvature perturbation at each point is a fixed function of the spectator's local value, given here to third order for a dominant curvaton and to first order for a modulated rate.
synthesis.imported-curvaton-and-modulate.lay: Two well-known proposals let a light field other than the one driving the universe's expansion set the primordial ripples: either it decays late and dominates for a while, or it controls how quickly the universe reheats. In both, the ripple at each place is a simple formula in that field's local value, and these are the formulas.

imported_from.citation: K.-Y. Choi and O. Seto, Modulated reheating by curvaton, Phys. Rev. D 85 (2012), 123528; arXiv:1204.1419.

synthesis.imported-de-sitter-invariant-h.formal:
Let $\phi$ be a free real scalar field of mass $m^{2} > 0$ (curvature coupling absorbed into $m^{2}$) on the de Sitter gravitational field of Hubble rate $H$ (a gravitational field on flat spacetime, Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}). The pure quasi-free states invariant under the connected de Sitter group form a one-complex-parameter family, the $\alpha$-vacua, obtained from the Euclidean state $\omega_{0}$ (the analytic continuation of the Euclidean theory on the sphere) by a frequency-independent Bogoliubov transformation; for real $\alpha$ their symmetric two-point functions are $G_{\alpha}(x,y) = \cosh 2\alpha\,G_{0}(x,y) + \sinh 2\alpha\,G_{0}(x, ar y)$, $ ar y$ the antipode of $y$. The Euclidean state is Hadamard; every other member is singular also at antipodal points, and since two Hadamard two-point functions differ by a smooth function, none of them is Hadamard. So for $m^{2} > 0$ the de Sitter-invariant Hadamard state is unique. In the flat slicing, with conformal time $\eta < 0$ and scale factor $a = -1/(H\eta)$, it is the Bunch-Davies state, the mode of the rescaled field $a\phi$ being $\chi_{k} \propto (-\eta)^{1/2}H^{(1)}_{
u}(-k\eta)$, $
u^{2} = 	frac94 - m^{2}/H^{2}$, whose large-argument expansion $H^{(1)}_{
u}(z) \sim \sqrt{2/\pi z}\,e^{I_4(z - 
u\pi/2 - \pi/4)} igl(1 + I_4(4
u^{2} - 1)/8z + O(z^{-2}) igr)$ fixes its short-distance behaviour (complex numbers, the mode functions' values among them, are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$, the field theory's complex field, conventions U1; the source writes $i$ for $I_4$). For the massless minimally coupled field there is no de Sitter-invariant Fock vacuum; states invariant under the Euclidean group $E(3)$ of the flat slicing exist, the Bunch-Davies state among them. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Allen1985}; \cite{BrunettiFredenhagenHollands2005} (the antipodal singularity and the failure of the Hadamard condition, as attributed there to Allen).

\emph{Note (the massless case; added 1 November).} The $E(3)$-invariant Bunch-Davies state of the massless minimally coupled field ($
u = 	frac32$) is infrared-divergent: its slice fields smeared with test functions of nonzero mean have infinite variance, those of zero mean or derivatives finite variance (Ford and Parker, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-ford-parker-infrared-divergence}). It is a state only on the algebra of the latter, and a comparison with it needs an infrared regularisation. The massive statement above, and the index-$2$ conclusion of the frozen-point reading of the descent, which uses it for fields with $m^{2} > 0$ (the conformal weight, $m^{2} = 2H^{2}$, $
u = 	frac12$, among them), are unaffected.
synthesis.imported-de-sitter-invariant-h.technical: A massive free field on de Sitter has many states that look the same at every point and in every direction, the $\alpha$-vacua, all related to the Euclidean (Bunch-Davies) state by one fixed mixing of positive and negative frequencies. Only the Euclidean state has the short-distance behaviour of the vacuum in flat spacetime, the Hadamard condition; every other member also correlates each point with its antipode singularly, so it cannot be a physically regular state. So the regular de Sitter-invariant state is unique. In the flat slicing its modes are Hankel functions, whose large-argument expansion gives its spectrum on scales well inside the horizon. For a massless minimally coupled field no fully de Sitter-invariant vacuum exists, only states invariant under the flat slicing's translations and rotations.
synthesis.imported-de-sitter-invariant-h.lay: In a universe expanding at a constant rate there is a whole family of states that each look like empty space everywhere. Allen showed that only one of them behaves like ordinary empty space at short distances; the others hide singular correlations between opposite points of the universe.

imported_from.citation: B. Allen, Vacuum states in de Sitter space, Phys. Rev. D 32 (1985), 3136--3149.
R. Brunetti, K. Fredenhagen and S. Hollands, A remark on alpha vacua for quantum field theories on de Sitter space, J. High Energy Phys. 2005, no. 05, 063; arXiv:hep-th/0503022.

synthesis.imported-ford-parker-infrared-.formal:
Let $\phi$ be a free real scalar field on a spatially flat Robertson-Walker gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) with conformal time $\eta$ and scale factor $a(\eta)$, and $\omega$ a homogeneous isotropic quasi-free state with mode functions $\chi_{k}(\eta)$ of $a\phi$ (Wronskian normalised), so that on a slice $\eta = \eta_{d}$ the smeared field $\phi(g) = \int g(\vec x)\phi(\eta_{d}, \vec x)\,d^{3}x$ has
\[
\omega(\phi(g)^{2}) = a(\eta_{d})^{-2}\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,|\hat g(\vec k)|^{2}\,|\chi_{k}(\eta_{d})|^{2}.
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(The criterion; Higuchi and Rendell, Sec.~3, four dimensions.)} If $|\chi_{k}(\eta_{d})|^{2} \ge c\,k^{-2\nu}$ on some $(0, k_{0})$ with $c > 0$ and $\nu \ge \tfrac32$, the momentum integral of the equal-time two-point function diverges at small $k$.
\item[(b)] \emph{(Ford and Parker.)} The massless minimally coupled field on the de Sitter field ($a = -1/(H\eta)$, mode index $\nu = \tfrac32$) in its Bunch-Davies state, and on a class of power-law Robertson-Walker fields in the corresponding homogeneous states, has an infrared-divergent two-point function.
\item[(c)] \emph{(Smeared slice fields; elementary.)} Under (a), $\omega(\phi(g)^{2}) = \infty$ for every test function $g$ of nonzero mean, $\int g \neq 0$, since $|\hat g|^{2}$ is continuous with value $|\int g|^{2}$ at $k = 0$; for $\tfrac32 \le \nu < \tfrac52$, $|\chi_{k}|^{2} \le C k^{-2\nu}$ near $k = 0$ and $|\chi_{k}|^{2}$ polynomially bounded at large $k$, every test function of zero mean gives a finite value, since then $|\hat g(\vec k)|^{2} \le C' k^{2}$. So such a state is not a state on the algebra of slice fields of nonzero mean; restricted to fields smeared with test functions of zero mean (or to derivatives of the field) it is.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Provenance:} \cite{FordParker1977}; \cite[Sec.~3]{HiguchiRendell2017}.
synthesis.imported-ford-parker-infrared-.technical: For a massless field with no coupling to the curvature, the natural homogeneous states of an expanding universe can carry so much power at the longest wavelengths that the field's correlation function does not exist: the integral over momenta diverges at small momenta. Ford and Parker found this in a class of power-law expanding universes, and it holds for the massless minimally coupled field in its Bunch-Davies state on de Sitter, where the mode functions grow as the inverse three-halves power of the momentum. In terms of smeared fields on a slice, a field averaged with a profile of nonzero total weight then has infinite variance, while profiles of zero total weight, or derivatives of the field, have finite variance. So, if the mode power grows at least that fast, the divergence is a statement about which observables the state is defined on.
synthesis.imported-ford-parker-infrared-.lay: In an expanding universe, a field of massless particles that ignores the curvature of space can pile up fluctuations on ever larger scales; if it does so fast enough, so much that the average value of the field over any region fluctuates infinitely. Ford and Parker found this in 1977. Differences of the field between nearby places stay finite, so the problem concerns only averages over regions. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: L. H. Ford and L. Parker, Infrared divergences in a class of Robertson-Walker universes, Phys. Rev. D 16 (1977), 245--250.
A. Higuchi and N. Rendell, Infrared divergences for free quantum fields in cosmological spacetimes, arXiv:1711.03964.

synthesis.imported-kaluza-klein-ansatz.formal:
Let a five-dimensional gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat $\R^{1,4}$ (the $d$-dimensional clause of Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) be independent of the fifth background coordinate $y$ and have the Kaluza-Klein form: for a background vector $a = \bar a + a^{y}e_{y}$ ($\bar a$ in the four background directions, $e_{y}$ the fifth),
\[
\hb^{-1}(a) \;=\; \hb_{4}^{-1}(\bar a) \;+\; \phi\,\bigl(a^{y} + \kappa\,A \cdot \bar a\bigr)\,e_{5},
\]
with $\hb_{4}$ a four-dimensional gravitational field, $A = A_{a}e^{a}$ a vector potential, $\phi$ the scale of the fifth direction and $e_{5}$ a unit physical vector orthogonal to the four physical directions, $\epsilon := Q(e_{5}) = \pm 1$ the sign fixed by the signature. Its derived metric is $g(a, b) = g_{4}(\bar a, \bar b) + \epsilon\,\phi^{2}(a^{y} + \kappa A \cdot \bar a)(b^{y} + \kappa A \cdot \bar b)$ (in components, $g_{ab} + \epsilon\kappa^{2}\phi^{2}A_{a}A_{b}$, $g_{ay} = \epsilon\kappa\phi^{2}A_{a}$, $g_{yy} = \epsilon\phi^{2}$; the source displays the case $\epsilon = +1$). Then the five-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action reduces, per unit length of $y$, to $S = -\int d^{4}x\,\det(\hb_{4})^{-1}\,\phi\,\bigl(\tfrac{R}{16\pi G} + \tfrac14\phi^{2}F_{ab}F^{ab} + \tfrac{2}{3\kappa^{2}}\,\partial_{a}\phi\,\partial^{a}\phi/\phi^{2}\bigr)$, with $R$ the scalar curvature of the derived four-dimensional metric in the review's sign: four-dimensional gravity, a Maxwell field $F = \nabla \wedge A$ (the bivector with components $F_{ab}$) whose kinetic term carries $\det(\hb_{4})^{-1}\phi^{3}$, and a scalar; the background displacements $y \mapsto y + \kappa\lambda(x)$ act on $A$ as gauge transformations $A \mapsto A - \nabla\lambda$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Kaluza1921}, \cite{Klein1926}; in the form of \cite{OverduinWesson1997} (eqs. (5), (9)).
synthesis.imported-kaluza-klein-ansatz.technical: Kaluza and Klein noticed that the part of a five-dimensional gravitational field that tilts the four physical directions into the fifth (the mixed components of its derived metric) behaves, in four dimensions, as an electromagnetic potential, and that coordinate changes along the fifth direction act on it as gauge transformations. Reducing the five-dimensional gravitational action gives four-dimensional gravity, a Maxwell field whose coupling depends on the size of the fifth direction (its kinetic term carries the cube of that size), and a scalar field for the size itself.
synthesis.imported-kaluza-klein-ansatz.lay: A century ago Kaluza and Klein showed that gravity in five dimensions looks, to four-dimensional observers, like gravity plus electromagnetism plus one extra field measuring the size of the hidden dimension. That bookkeeping is what lets one read part of a five-dimensional gravitational field as a four-dimensional vector field.

imported_from.citation: T. Kaluza, Zum Unitaetsproblem der Physik, Sitzungsber. Preuss. Akad. Wiss. Berlin (Math. Phys.) 1921, 966--972.
O. Klein, Quantentheorie und fuenfdimensionale Relativitaetstheorie, Z. Phys. 37 (1926), 895--906.
J. M. Overduin and P. S. Wesson, Kaluza-Klein gravity, Phys. Rep. 283 (1997), 303--378; arXiv:gr-qc/9805018.
